title: TDDR Rising Narratives — Sunday evening, Nov 15
summary: A snapshot of opposition narratives from the Right and the Far Left as of 5:30 PM ET Sunday, Nov 15, 2026. Built for TDDR (Too Dumb Didn't Read). Since this morning, three new Right-wing frames took off: 'Democrats want to bring back USAID' (5,025 posts in 24 hours, 3.13× its prior daily average); 'Slotkin is a CIA asset running a color revolution' (2,978 posts, 8.52×, the steepest acceleration in the set); and Trump's revived 'Seditious Six' attack, which picked up an unverified money-laundering rumor. 'Democrats are coming for your paycheck' kept growing, from 1,780 posts in this morning's window to 3,310. On the left, NYC-DSA's vote urging Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez to run in 2028 and Rep.-elect Don Leonard's conditions for backing Hakeem Jeffries joined the leadership fights, and Van Hollen vs. Schumer stayed the largest conversation after the Sunday shows. The FAA story is cooling now that the agency says in writing it has 'no indication' of a cyberattack. Every count, quote, and fact-check comes from sources and X queries pulled this evening or this morning. Nothing here is invented.

trends.detail: U.S. trends were pulled at about 5:12 PM ET with x.get_trends_by_woeid (WOEID 23424977, max 50; 50 returned). NFL Sunday dominated the list (teams, players, coaches, and fan hashtags), along with 'England' and 'Spain.' None of the thirteen narratives we scored appeared on the U.S. trends list this evening, so no card received the trend bonus. We requested tweet_count, but the trend objects did not include it, so trend volumes are unavailable and we did not estimate them.

countsPulledLabel: Post counts and samples pulled between about 5:13 and 5:30 PM ET Sunday
hottestQueryDetail: Van Hollen vs. Schumer (27,659 posts in the last 24 hours)
factCheckOutletsDetail: FAA (official), AP, Axios, Just The News, Carnegie Endowment event record, Tax Foundation (carried over from this morning)

oppositionNote.body: Right = narratives the Right is pushing after the Democratic midterm wave. Far Left = pressure on Democratic leadership and the incoming majority from the party's left. Several stories tonight are worked by both sides: the Right amplifies the NYC-DSA vote and Don Leonard's 'living hell' quote as a 'Democratic civil war,' and Slotkin is a target in two separate Right-wing cards. The tag is the primary opposition frame.

methodology: Last updated Sunday, Nov 15, 2026, 5:30 PM ET. This is a research snapshot for TDDR, not a live API, and it will go stale overnight. U.S. X trends were pulled at about 5:12 PM ET. This morning's snapshot (Nov 15, 7:22 AM ET) is kept in the archive and was not overwritten. Eight of its eleven narratives were re-counted with the same queries so momentum compares like with like. Three were dropped because they faded: Thune's adjournment (509 posts in the last 24 hours), 'Jeffries wants to pay deported DACA recipients' (245), and Al Green's impeachment push (306). Five new narratives were added with new queries: USAID, Slotkin's 'color revolution,' the Seditious Six, NYC-DSA and Ocasio-Cortez, and Don Leonard.

For each narrative we ran one English-language X search with x.get_posts_counts_recent at hourly granularity. We counted matches in a window from 5:00 PM ET Saturday, Nov 14, through 5:00 PM ET Sunday, Nov 15 (exactly 24 hours), and over a 167-hour 'seven-day' window from 6:00 PM ET Sunday, Nov 8 (the earliest whole-hour start the recent-count API allowed at pull time) to the same end point. We tightened the Slotkin query (adding -seditious and dropping bare 'CIA') after a first version overlapped heavily with Seditious Six template posts; only the tightened query's counts are used. We counted named news or fact-check outlets whose coverage we opened or retrieved in this evening's searches and cite on the card. Official government pages, think-tank event pages, X News summaries, and X posts are cited as sources but not counted as outlets, and sources carried over from this morning without being re-retrieved are not counted. We noted whether each topic appeared on the U.S. trends list at about 5:12 PM ET.

Score = 50% volume index + 30% acceleration index + 20% coverage index. Volume index is 100 × log10(1 + last-24h posts) / log10(1 + the highest last-24h count in this set). Acceleration index is 100 × min(last-24h / prior daily average, 3) / 3, so a triple-or-higher average scores 100. Prior daily average is (seven-day total − last 24h) / 6. Coverage index is 70 × min(outlets, 7) / 7, plus 30 if the topic was on the U.S. X trends list this evening. Morning-to-evening score changes reflect both volume and how much coverage we retrieved, so read the post counts alongside the scores.

Counts are query matches, not unique posts or unique users, and queries can overlap. The filibuster query excludes SAVE Act posts, the Slotkin query excludes 'seditious,' and the Leonard query includes the bare name 'Leonard' (every post in our sample was about Don Leonard). Replies are included, and automated @grok replies make up a visible share of several queries. Sentiment is a qualitative label from relevancy-sorted post samples and from quotes in news coverage, not a scientific poll. The filibuster and Medicare for All cards did not get a fresh sample tonight, and they say so. Daily bar charts use UTC days (a UTC day starts at 7:00 PM ET the previous evening). Bars marked * are partial windows. Hourly charts are labeled in ET.

noFactCheckNote: If a card has no fact-check row, we did not find a rated fact-check for the core claim in this snapshot — not that the claim is true.
feedCaption: Thirteen narratives, scored inside this Sunday-evening set. Open a card for talking points, amplifiers, and sources.

disinfo.caption: Claims in this snapshot that have a fact-check, an official statement, or reporting we opened.
disinfo.caveatLead: A fact-check is not a volume score.
disinfo.caveatBody: New tonight: posts calling Sen. Elissa Slotkin 'a CIA asset' running a 'color revolution' recast a public Carnegie Endowment democracy event as a coup plan. The claim is unsupported, and we found no fact-check outlet rating it. An offshoot of Trump's 'Seditious Six' posts claims all six lawmakers ran a 'money laundering scheme.' It traces to partisan sites citing a 'Bob Cushman,' and we found no FEC action, charge, or fact-check, so treat it as unverified. A grand jury declined to indict the six in February. 'Democrats want to restore USAID' is missing context: Democrats plan oversight hearings, but we found no bill to recreate the agency. The weekend's most widely shared false claim, that Friday's FAA ground stop was a cyberattack, now has a written FAA denial ('no indication'), though the root-cause investigation is still open. 'Tax hikes on Americans' still compresses a debate over taxing high earners and corporations. Posts saying Ayanna Pressley has launched a speaker bid are still false; a town hall is not a candidacy. We also saw renewed rumors that Trump is dead or in a bunker, which we did not score as an opposition narrative. Per X News, Trump posted from the White House Sunday morning that he was holding meetings.

narratives.title: NEW: 'Democrats want to bring back USAID' — DOGE's greatest hits return after the midterms
narratives.query: (USAID) (Democrats OR Musk OR grants OR Congress) lang:en
narratives.sentimentNote: In a relevancy sample of Saturday-evening-to-Sunday posts, the top posts were list-style recaps of 2025 DOGE findings ('Here's a look back at the programs Elon Musk discovered') under the headline that Democrats want USAID back, plus copy-paste versions from smaller accounts. A visible minority of replies pushed back, asking for receipts or noting that a list of disliked grants is not evidence of fraud. This is a read of that sample, not a poll.
narratives.summary: The biggest new Right narrative tonight: 5,025 posts in the last 24 hours, 3.13 times its prior daily average. Hourly counts jumped from 26 to 284 and then 411 posts between 6 and 8 PM ET Saturday, right after @WallStreetApes posted 'NEW: Democrats are talking about restoring USAID after their Midterms win' with a recap of grants Elon Musk's DOGE flagged in 2025. That post had 5,576 likes, 3,205 reposts, and 72,602 views when we opened it, and a second wave built Sunday from late morning into the afternoon. X News clustered the story Sunday as 'USAID Spending Draws Renewed Criticism After Democrats' Midterm Wins,' repeating grant examples such as $1.5 million for a Serbian LGBTQ group, $2 million for sex-change procedures in Guatemala, and $20 million for a Sesame Street program in Iraq. The reporting we found is more cautious. Reuters reported after the election that many Democrats 'say they will try to restore funding' for foreign aid. Devex reports incoming committee leaders plan oversight hearings on how USAID was dismantled. Just The News reports that Democrats 'aren't saying they would restore USAID funding' and are focused on investigating Musk's role. We found no reported bill to recreate USAID.
talkingPoints: Democrats haven't even been sworn in and they want to restart the USAID slush fund.
Musk exposed it; Democrats want to bring it back.
Sesame Street in Iraq and sex changes in Guatemala — while veterans sleep on the street.
USAID needs to be banned for life, not rebooted.
narratives.amplifiers: Named accounts in posts we opened: @WallStreetApes (5,576 likes, 3,205 reposts, 72,602 views); copy-paste versions from @drscottYoung963 (30 likes, 359 views) and @monica_tvshow (13 likes, 314 views); and X News's Sunday summary quoting an unnamed congressional critic who said colleagues are 'really mad at Mr. Musk.'
narratives.whyItWorks: It reruns a fight the Right already won on social media, with ready-made receipts, and points it at the new majority. Foreign aid is unpopular in the abstract, and 'they want it back' doesn't require anyone to have actually proposed it.
narratives.audience: MAGA-aligned and DOGE-supporting voters, veterans' advocates who respond to the 'America first' contrast, and swing voters skeptical of foreign aid.
narratives.counter: Separate oversight from restoration. Incoming chairs have promised hearings on whether USAID's shutdown broke the law, but nobody has filed a bill to recreate the agency, and Trump can veto foreign-aid spending through 2028. On the grant list, ask for the amount, the year, and the agency before arguing the merits. Several of these were 2025 talking points that drew corrections at the time.

factChecks.claim: Democrats are moving to restore USAID after winning the midterms.
factChecks.detail: Reuters reported that many Democrats angered by the cuts 'say they will try to restore funding' for foreign aid, and Devex reports incoming chairs such as Rep. Gregory Meeks plan oversight hearings. Just The News reports Democrats 'aren't saying they would restore USAID funding.' We found no bill or leadership plan to recreate the agency. This is TDDR's read of that reporting, not a rating from a fact-check outlet.

narratives.title: NEW: 'Slotkin is a CIA asset running a color revolution' — a democracy speech recast as a coup plan
narratives.query: Slotkin ("CIA asset" OR "color revolution" OR reimagine OR reimagining OR "Trump proof" OR "Trump-proof" OR "after Trump") -seditious lang:en
narratives.sentimentNote: In a relevancy sample of the last 24 hours, the top original post called Sen. Elissa Slotkin 'a CIA asset whose job is to tear down our Constitution' and the clip 'the pitch for the Color Revolution to destroy the USA.' Most other matches were low-follower replies to Slotkin and to conservative influencers repeating 'CIA' and 'color revolution,' some calling for her to be jailed. This is a read of that sample, not a poll.
narratives.summary: The steepest acceleration in tonight's set: 2,978 posts in the last 24 hours, 8.52 times its prior daily average of about 350. This wasn't a one-post spike: volume held between roughly 115 and 175 posts an hour most of Saturday evening and Sunday. The trigger is a clip of Slotkin, a former CIA analyst, saying 'there is going to be an America after President Trump' and that leaders must 'reimagine and build something new' because 'the systems of the past are failing us,' as quoted by YubNub News. The remarks appear to trace to her Sept. 30 speech and conversation with Anne Applebaum at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, billed as lessons from Hungary and Poland on defending democracy. X News describes it as a video she shared this week. Right-wing sites, including Talk Red, frame her Europe trip as a 'color revolution strategy,' while Diplomacy Dish and News House argue the Carnegie tape 'undercuts coup hysteria.' This narrative is merging with Trump's renewed 'Seditious Six' attack, since Slotkin is one of the six.
talkingPoints: Slotkin is ex-CIA, and there's no such thing as ex-CIA.
'Reimagine the systems' means tear up the Constitution.
This is the color-revolution playbook from Eastern Europe, now on American soil.
She went to Hungary and Poland to learn how to take down a government.
narratives.amplifiers: Named accounts in posts we opened: @Keltic_Spirit (219 likes, 131 reposts, 2,213 views) with the 'CIA asset' framing; replies to @GuntherEagleman and to Slotkin's own account; and articles from Talk Red and YubNub News. X News summarized the reaction Sunday.
narratives.whyItWorks: It fuses a true biographical fact (she worked at the CIA) with a vague quote ('build something new') and an existing Right-wing frame ('color revolution'). Listeners can fill a vague quote with their worst fears, and the biography makes the conspiracy feel like evidence.
narratives.audience: MAGA-aligned and conspiracy-curious audiences, Trump supporters primed by the 'Seditious Six' posts, and some anti-establishment voters on the left who distrust the intelligence agencies.
narratives.counter: Play the tape; don't paraphrase it. The Carnegie event was about broad coalitions, anti-corruption cases, and free elections, the same tools the Right praised when they were used against governments it opposed. Don't defend vague language, either. Ask Slotkin to name the 'systems' she means.

factChecks.claim: Slotkin's call to 'reimagine and build something new' after Trump is a CIA-run 'color revolution' plan to overthrow the government.
factChecks.detail: The remarks appear to come from a public Carnegie Endowment event billed as lessons from Hungary and Poland on defending democracy. Her office's summary describes building coalitions, exposing corruption, and protecting free elections. Posts making the 'CIA asset' claim offered no evidence beyond her past CIA employment. We found no fact-check outlet rating the claim; this is TDDR's read of the event record and the coverage we retrieved.

narratives.hourlyNote: Hourly X post counts for this query, labeled in ET. The window runs from 5:00 PM ET Saturday, Nov 14, through 5:00 PM ET Sunday, Nov 15. The first '5 PM' bar is Saturday; the last '4 PM' bar is Sunday. Volume stayed elevated around the clock, dipping only in the early-morning hours, which points to a broad reply-driven narrative rather than one viral post. The query excludes 'seditious' to limit overlap with the Seditious Six card.

narratives.title: 'Democrats are coming for your paycheck' — the WSJ tax story gets a second wind Sunday
narratives.query: ("tax hike" OR "tax hikes" OR "raise taxes" OR "raising taxes" OR "tax increases" OR "39.6") (Democrats OR Democrat OR Dems) lang:en
narratives.sentimentNote: In a relevancy sample of Sunday posts (7 AM to 5 PM ET), conservative posts mocked Democrats' affordability message ('Here's my AFFORDABILITY shocked face'), and others warned that '39.6% is back on the table.' A few explainer-style posts accurately described the report as a debate over taxing high earners and corporations, and automated @grok replies again corrected the 'tax hikes on Americans' framing. This is a read of that sample, not a poll.
narratives.summary: Still the strongest carry-over from this morning, and growing: 3,310 posts in the last 24 hours, up from 1,780 in the morning window, at 6.72 times its prior daily average. Saturday night's spike (284 posts at 9 PM ET) eased overnight. A second wave built from 10 AM to 1 PM ET Sunday, peaking at 240 posts an hour. X News updated its cluster at about 4 PM ET with a hook saying Democrats are 'weighing tax hikes on Americans and corporations,' which keeps the broad framing in circulation. The underlying Wall Street Journal report, as quoted by Political Wire, says Democrats have 'a broad consensus to reverse President Trump’s tariffs' and the cuts to Medicaid, food stamps, and health subsidies, and that 'party lawmakers are weighing when to attach tax increases.' Options in circulation include a 39.6 percent top rate, a corporate rate 'in the mid-20s,' and higher capital-gains taxes for high earners. Nothing has been introduced, and any bill would face Trump's veto.
talkingPoints: Democrats won on affordability, and their first idea is raising your taxes.
39.6% is back on the table before they're even sworn in.
A $5 trillion wish list means tax hikes for everyone, not just billionaires.
Reversing Trump's tariffs and tax cuts is a tax increase by another name.
narratives.amplifiers: Named accounts in posts we opened Sunday: @MoniFunGirl (50 likes, 613 views), @Cmfover84 ('39.6% is back on the table,' 397 views), and @PatriotAndPoise. X News kept its cluster updated through Sunday afternoon. We did not re-check this morning's amplifiers (@Bubblebathgirl, @AlphaWireHQ).
narratives.whyItWorks: Affordability won Democrats the midterms, so 'they'll raise your taxes' attacks the brand at its strongest point. It's also partly true — Democrats are debating tax increases — which makes the exaggeration ('on Americans') harder to rebut in one line.
narratives.audience: Conservative and libertarian voters, small-business owners, and swing voters who backed Democrats on costs. Also likely to resonate with moderate Democrats wary of the party's left.
narratives.counter: Say who pays. The proposals on the table target incomes over roughly $1 million and corporations, and Trump can veto all of it until 2029. Put the trade on the table plainly: restoring Medicaid, SNAP, and ACA subsidies for working families, paid for by the top bracket. Don't deny that a debate over tax increases is happening — it is.

factChecks.claim: Democrats are planning 'major tax hikes on Americans' for 2027.
factChecks.detail: The Wall Street Journal report, as quoted by Political Wire, says Democrats are 'weighing when to attach tax increases' to bills reversing Medicaid, SNAP, and health-subsidy cuts — a debate, not a passed plan. The Tax Foundation says the proposals on the table target high-income individuals and corporations and that any tax increase is 'limited by President Trump’s veto.' Viral posts dropped both caveats. This is TDDR's read of that reporting, not a rating from a fact-check outlet.

narratives.hourlyNote: Hourly X post counts for this query, labeled in ET. The window runs from 5:00 PM ET Saturday, Nov 14, through 5:00 PM ET Sunday, Nov 15. narratives.title: Van Hollen vs. Schumer — an 'exit ramp' for Fetterman, '15 and growing,' and a DSA question on Fox
narratives.query: ("Van Hollen" OR VanHollen) (Schumer OR "majority leader" OR leader OR challenge OR challenging OR bid) lang:en
narratives.sentimentNote: In a relevancy sample of Sunday posts (7 AM to 5 PM ET), supporters shared Van Hollen's claim that he is at 'about 15 and growing' and told senators that endorsing Schumer is now 'unforgivable,' while news accounts circulated the Washington Post's report that few colleagues immediately embraced him. Right-leaning accounts focused on the Fox News Sunday DSA exchange and on Fetterman. This is a read of that sample, not a poll.
narratives.summary: Still the largest conversation by volume: 27,659 posts in the last 24 hours, flat against 27,849 in this morning's window, at 1.06 times its prior daily average. Hourly counts rose from about 360 an hour before dawn to nearly 2,000 an hour between noon and 2 PM ET as Sunday-show clips spread. On Fox News Sunday, Van Hollen said Sen. John Fetterman is 'worried about a Democratic primary' and is 'maybe looking for an exit ramp,' and that 'American taxpayers should not be providing a blank check to the government of Israel or any government,' Newsweek reports. X News says he was also asked about members of the Democratic Socialists of America and said the party should welcome all voices. Politico reports Van Hollen disputes Schumer's claim that he has the votes to stay leader. The caucus votes Dec. 1.
talkingPoints: Van Hollen is at 15 and growing — Schumer's 'committed list' is a bluff.
Fetterman wants an exit ramp; let him take it.
No blank checks for any government — that's what voters elected us to say.
Call your senator before Dec. 1.
narratives.amplifiers: Named voices in coverage and posts we opened: Sen. Chris Van Hollen on Fox News Sunday, per Newsweek; Sen. John Fetterman's Saturday interview with Kayleigh McEnany; @SimplySubstance's '15 and growing' clip (69 likes, 22 reposts, 3,702 views); and @PollTracker2024 sharing the Washington Post's 'few colleagues' report (120 likes, 17,117 views).
narratives.whyItWorks: A leadership race stays alive when every senator becomes a target. Van Hollen's public whip count, even unverified, turns a closed-ballot vote into a public scoreboard, and the Fetterman and DSA exchanges let both progressives and the Right frame it as a fight over the party's identity.
narratives.audience: Progressive Democrats and anti-war voters pushing to replace Schumer; pro-Israel Democrats alarmed by the Fetterman clip; and right-leaning accounts treating it as proof of a Democratic civil war.
narratives.counter: Separate the claims from the count. Van Hollen says he has about 15; Schumer has more than a dozen public backers and says he has the votes. Neither list is verified. Before Dec. 1, ask both for specifics: a yes or no on the filibuster and a first-100-days bill list.

narratives.title: FAA ground stop, Sunday evening: the FAA rules out a cyberattack in writing, and the fight shifts to 'botched upgrade' and Buttigieg
narratives.query: (FAA OR "ground stop" OR "air traffic" OR groundstop) (Buttigieg OR "Mayor Pete" OR cyberattack OR "cyber attack" OR hacked OR sabotage) lang:en
narratives.sentimentNote: In a relevancy sample of Sunday posts (7 AM to 5 PM ET), most posts accepted the official account ('not a cyber attack, just maintenance gone wrong') and moved on to blame: a 'botched routine upgrade' of 'ancient copper wiring,' the Biden-era FAA, and the 'Mayor Pete' callback to American Airlines' Christmas Eve 2024 ground stop. A smaller set kept up the 'they aren't telling you everything' framing. This is a read of that sample, not a poll.
narratives.summary: Still a top story by volume, but cooling: 11,592 posts in the last 24 hours, down from 14,455 in this morning's window, at 2.12 times its prior daily average. Its score fell from 91 this morning to 73. New Sunday: the FAA published a Q&A saying 'we have no indication that this was a cyberattack or an outside nefarious actor' and that the SMART tool 'does not feed information into the air traffic control system.' The FAA says data flooded its network at '1,000 connection attempts every 4 to 5 seconds' from two sites: a radar site in Amarillo, Texas, and a radio site in El Dorado, Arkansas, where L3Harris had deployed a new router. It says it disabled the same function on about 60 similar routers and is still investigating the root cause. The FAA counts about 12,462 flights canceled Friday, not all of them because of the ground stop. Airways Magazine reports that Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy told ABC's This Week he expects operations to be fully normal Monday.
talkingPoints: It was a botched contractor upgrade on a system Buttigieg left to rot.
Remember Christmas Eve 2024? Nobody blamed Mayor Pete then.
Give Duffy the money and finish air traffic control modernization.
They say 'no cyberattack' every time — the investigation isn't finished.
narratives.amplifiers: Named voices in coverage and posts we opened: the FAA's Sunday Q&A; Secretary Duffy on ABC's This Week, per Airways Magazine; @ToscaAusten's 'Mayor Pete' Christmas Eve post (31 likes, 28 reposts, 704 views); @shadowgrid7's 'They aren't telling you everything'; and a Just the News story, shared on X, about the White House Rapid Response account blaming the Biden-era FAA. Automated @grok replies remain a visible share of matches.
narratives.whyItWorks: A miserable travel weekend needs a villain, and the official explanation hands each side one: the Right gets a contractor, a decades-old system, and a funding ask, plus the 'Mayor Pete did it too' callback; Democrats get a resignation demand and an oversight hook.
narratives.audience: Pro-administration posters defending Duffy, conservative media audiences, travelers still caught in the recovery, and Democrats preparing January oversight.
narratives.counter: Use the FAA's own words: two sites, one contractor, about 60 routers patched, and a root cause still under investigation. 'No indication of a cyberattack' is the official position, and so is 'still investigating.' On Buttigieg: the 2024 Christmas Eve stop was one airline's vendor outage, not a failure of the national airspace system. Ask for a date for the final report.

factChecks.claim: A cyberattack caused Friday's nationwide FAA ground stop.
factChecks.rating: False, per the FAA — root-cause investigation still open
factChecks.detail: The FAA's Sunday Q&A says 'Based on all available evidence, we have no indication that this was a cyberattack or an outside nefarious actor,' and traces the data flood to two sites, including one where L3Harris deployed a new router. The FAA and L3Harris 'continue to investigate the root cause,' and no final report has been published. This restates the official position; we did not independently verify it.

factChecks.claim: The FAA's new AI-assisted SMART system caused the ground stop.
factChecks.detail: The FAA's Sunday Q&A says 'The two systems are not related. SMART is a data aggregator, and it does not feed information into the air traffic control system.' We did not independently verify the vendor architecture; this rating restates the agency's denial.

narratives.summary: 2,464 posts in the last 24 hours, 1.31 times its prior daily average. This is a second wave. The six are Sens. Elissa Slotkin and Mark Kelly and Reps. Jason Crow, Chris Deluzio, Chrissy Houlahan, and Maggie Goodlander, who made a November 2025 video telling service members they can refuse illegal orders. AP and CBS News reported that a federal grand jury declined to indict them on Feb. 10, 2026. Crow responded that Trump 'can bring it on,' and Slotkin said, 'Bring it.' On Sunday, an offshoot claim that 'every single one of the Seditious Six' was involved in a 'money laundering scheme,' attributed to a 'Bob Cushman,' spread through @DeepLeaksHQ (451 likes, 319 reposts, 5,839 views) and sites such as Headline USA.

Telling troops to disobey orders is sedition, period.
Justice is coming for the traitors.

Jason Crow and Sen. Elissa Slotkin responding, per Joe.My.God.
narratives.whyItWorks: A presidential post turns a year-old video into fresh content, and the 'seditious' label works like an indictment without one. The money-laundering offshoot shows how a dormant accusation picks up new, unverified charges as it recirculates.
narratives.audience: Trump's base, military and veteran audiences sensitive to questions of orders and discipline, and MAGA influencers who amplify Truth Social posts.
narratives.counter: Lead with the outcome: a grand jury heard the government's case and declined to indict. The video restated that troops can refuse unlawful orders, which is already military law. On the laundering claim, ask for the FEC filing or the charge. We found neither.
